label: paragraph_title
text: NOTE TO PEKING.

label: text
text:
British Minister on Wanhsen.
YANG SEN'S ACT OF PIRACY.

label: text
text: The Note of His Majesty's Minister states that he has the honor to acknowledge the receipt of the Walchitopu's "memorandio" on September 10 and 14 on the subject of the seizure of the British merchant steamers at Wanhien, in which four complaints were made against the British steamers in connection with the sinking of junks of the Upper Yangtse as follows: Firstly, "the steamer "Tienkuang" on June 13 in the district of Wanhien, secondly the "Wanliu" on June 8 in the district of Fengju; thirdly, the "Chiall" on August 2 at Foutan; and fourthly, the "Wanliu" on August 29 at Yungyang.

label: text
text: Owing to the Interruption of regular communications, due to civil war conditions on the Yangtse, and the fact that His Majesty's Consul at Chungking is at present at Ichang, the British Minister hitherto has only been able to obtain telegraphic reports regarding these cases, but the British Consul at Chungking states that of the four cases alleged the first was never reported to him, the second was completely refuted, and the third was referred to the Steamship Company concerned for observation.

label: text
text: As regards the fourth the British Consul; on the day after the occurrence, telegraphed to General Yang Sen that any claim against the "Wanliu" should be brought through his Consulate, when it would be promptly and equitably dealt with, and in view of Yang Sen's high-handed detention of two British ships, which were not connected with the Yungyang incident he forthwith proceeded to Wanhsien in order to deal with the matter personally.

label: text
text: The British Minister has already discussed this last Wanhsien case and the grave incidents arising therefrom, and now places on record the following outline of the facts as they have hitherto reached him:—

label: text
text: The "Wanliu" on August 29 was discharging passengers at Yung-yang when she was boarded by sixteen armed soldiers seeking to commandeer accommodation for the transport of Chinese troops in violation of the regulations prohibiting British vessels, in the interests of strict neutrality in Chinese civil wars, from carrying armed Chinese forces, whilst simultaneously sampans containing troops approached the ship.

label: text
text:
Proper Legal Inquiry.
The “Wanliu” proceeded slowly in order to avoid the sampan when fire was opened from both banks of the Yangtse River and the troops on board rushed the bridge and engine-room, but fortunately were driven off by the ship's officers. Sampans endeavouring to come alongside the vessel fouled one another and eventually sank. On arrival at Wanhsien the troops were removed from the “Wanliu” by H.M.S. “Cockchafer” and the “Wanliu” proceeded on her voyage. On August 29 Yang Sen, apparently, as a reprisal, seized the “Wanhsien” and “Wantung,” putting at least 300 soldiers aboard. Yang Sen declined to discuss the matter with the commander of the “Cockchafer” whereupon the Consul hurried from Chungking to Wanhsien to take charge of the negotiations. Yang Sen refused to listen to his representations or release the steamers or the officers until the matter of “Wanliu” was settled. The Consul, acting under instructions from the Minister, in Peking, exhausted every possible conciliatory effort, including, naturally, an offer of a proper legal inquiry. Yang Sen declined to agree to any terms which did not permit him to exact compensation from the Company without regard to the actual facts of the case.
On September 5, H.M.S. "Widgeon" and the "Kiawo" the latter manned by four naval officers and 60 men, proceeded to Wanhsien to assist the "Cockchafer" in effecting the release of the ships and officers.

label: text
text:
Strict British Neutrality.
As she approached the detained vessels the “Kiawo” met with murderous rifle and machine-gun fire without warning from the Chinese soldiers. Other British vessels were subjected to heavy rifle and field-gun fire from the troops

label: text
text: TO-DAY'S CEREMONY

label: text
text: St. John's Cathedral was the scene this afternoon of a pretty military wedding attended by officers of the 1st Battalion, East Surrey Regiment, members of the Sergeant's Mess and their wives.

label: text
text: The parties were Miss Dorothy Rose Oram, daughter of Sergt. and Mrs. Oram, of the Ast Battalion East Surreys; and Sergt. Frederick Charles Ridger, also of the 1st Battalion, East Surreys, and Mrs. and Mrs. Ridger, of Addestone. Surrey.

label: text
text: Both bride and bridegroom are very popular in the Regiment with which they have been connected for some considerable time. the bride having been born whilst the Regiment was in Jersey.

label: text
text: The Rev. G. F. Stopford, chaplain to the troops in Hong Kong, officiated.

label: text
text: The bride, who entered the church on the arm of her father, by whom she was given away, wore a becoming dress of velvet georgette and carried a bouquet of white roses.

label: text
text:
Miss Lily May Orum, her sister, who was bridesmaid, wore a dress of blue taffeta and carried a pretty bouquet of carnations.
The bride's mother was attired in peach coloured georgette:
Sergeant Bays, of the 1st Battalion, East Surrey Regiment, was the best man.

label: text
text: After a reception at the quarters-in-Kennedy Road, the happy couple leave for their honeymoon at Repulse Bay, the bride's travelling dress being of flowered voile with hat to match.

label: text
text: The bride's gift to the bride-groom was a gold signet ring and that of the bridegroom to the bride a gold slave bangle.

The gunboats, in self-defence, were compelled to return fire against this point, including the town of Wanhien, from which they were being attacked and ultimately went down river, having effected the release of five of the six officers. The sixth was reported to have been wounded and presumed to have been drowned.
The British Minister quotes the British casualties and goes on:—Pending the receipt of instructions the British Minister reserves, on behalf of His Majesty's Government, all their rights in connection with this grave incident. Meantime he draws the attention of the Wachiaopu to the fact that the immediate cause was the high-handed action of the Chinese military officer in attempting to commandeer a British ship for the transport of troops, and that the British Government, in pursuance of strict neutrality in Chinese civil wars, has consistently refused all British ships to be so used.

label: text
text:
Strong Ignition Words.
The Note points out Yang Sen's proper procedure, if he had a real or fancied cause of complaint. "It emphasises that the Chinese militaries place themselves entirely in the wrong if they endeavour to exact reparation by such menns as the forcible detention of British ships not connected with the case. It goes on:—His Majesty's Government is quite unable to tolerate such action. Yang Sen must be aware of the correct procedure in cases where he has a complaint against British subjects or ships. His action in seizing ships and posting armed soldiers aboard who open fire on British gunboats amounts to nothing less than piracy."
His Majesty's Minister is convinced that the Walchinopu will not attempt to defend it. The Wachiapupu may rest assured that His Majesty's officers will endeavour to arrange on the spot an amicable solution of the difficulties which have arisen in connection with the case; but as a preliminary to discussion, it is essential that the two detained ships be handed over forthwith to the British authorities.
(Signed) Ronald MacLeny.
Peking, September 20.

label: paragraph_title
text: NO POWER?

label: paragraph_title
text: Local Law & Chinese Pirates.

label: text
text: VITAL POINT RAISED.

label: text
text: Does Our Jurisdiction Extend to China?

label: text
text: In connection with the charge of piracy against three Chinese at the Criminal Sessions there was an interesting development this morning when Mr. C. G. Alebaster K.C., submitted that the court had no jurisdiction over Chinese subjects alleged to be implicated in piracy in Chinese waters.

label: text
text: The alleged piracy occurred off Cheung Chau Island, four miles outside the limits of British waters.

label: text
text:
Mr. Alabaster submitted that the prisoners had no case to answer. (They have not yet given their evidence).
It had been proved beyond contest that the spot where the attack by the “white sail” sampant took place was within Chinese waters, said Mr. Alabaster.
For the purpose of his own argument, continued counsel, he would not contend that beyond the ultimate coasts of China there was a territorial jurisdiction extending over three or four miles. It would be sufficient for his purposes that the alleged piracy had taken place in Chinese territory without the additional mileage.

label: text
text: The spot in question was as much within the body of the county or district of China, continued counsel, as the Solent was within the body of Southampton and the Bristol Channel within the county of Glamorgan.

label: paragraph_title
text: JURY PRIVACY.

label: paragraph_title
text:
NEED FOR REFORM LOCALLY.
READER'S COMPLAINT

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mail"] Sir,—As a member of the public interested in the murder trial which concluded yesterday I attended the court throughout the morning and was extremely surprised at the lack of adequate jury facilities.

label: text
text: In the first place, the jury when retiring to consider its verdict, passes through the public corridor and yesterday I observed a Chinese woman stop and address a member of the jury as he was on his way, with the others, to consider the verdict.

label: text
text: The staring crowd outside the windows of the room yesterday grew to such dimensions and members of it were so persistent in their attentions that, quite properly, the jury sent out a message asking that the verandah in question should be cleared.

label: text
text: This was in fact, done at the order of the usher but as the usher's duty is to remain at the door of the room, some distance away and out of sight of the verandah windows, the clearance was only temporary.

label: text
text:
As a member of a former jury which also experienced considerable annoyance as a result of the attentions of a curious crowd in our deliberations on an equally grave occasion, I consider that the least the law which calls on them to adjudicate in an issue of life and death can do for them is to provide privacy during their deliberations.
In courts at Home the jury have a special entrance and exit which ensures that in leaving the court they are unmolested and the room with which they are provided is secure against all would-be evas-droppers or observers.

label: text
text:
Hong Kong, September 22.
[The above letter was submitted by the “China Mail” this morning to the Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp, Attorney General. Mr. Kemp said that the matter merited serious consideration and he would bring it to the attention of the Chief Justice. A room which provided more privacy than the one in present was the Chief Justice's Clerk's room which some time ago had been used for this purpose — Editor, “China Mail.”

label: paragraph_title
text: WAR ZONE SHIFTS.

label: text
text: CHANG KAI-SHEK'S STRATEGIC ADVANTAGE:

label: text
text: WU CHANGES HIS MIND.

label: text
text:
[By Our Special Correspondent.]
Latest movements in the central China war portend the shifting of the main scene of hostilities from Hupeh province to Kiangsi.

label: text
text: The lull in the Nationalists v. Sun Chuan-fang zone continues with the southerners moving up troops as though preparatory to striking. Marshal Sun Chuan-fang's "five provinces" are still rushing up reinforcements towards the more flexible parts of their line.

label: text
text: Despatches from Kiangsi point to General Chang Kai-shek having taken up the position of a semi-circle, the middle of which threatens Nanchang. the capital of Kiangsi province.

label: text
text: The southern main force is in the centre of a large salient, having “bent back” the Kiangsi garrison to an extent whereby fresh divisions can be pushed forward rapidly to any part of the semi-circle.

label: text
text: Previous hesitation on the part of Marshal Sun Chuan-fang is blamed for having given the Nationalists this big advantage.

label: text
text: Military experts predict that Sun Chuan-fang will not fight seriously at least till another week

label: text
text: has passed by, when he will have put sufficient troops in the field to ensure numerical superiority over the southerners.

label: text
text: He is still waiting for Marshal Chang Tso-lin of Fengtien to give evidence of good faith as a professed ally, by taking the field in the north, on Wu Pei-fu's side. Native peace missions are still relying on Sun Chuan-fang's suspicions of a "back door" attack by Chang Tso-lin, and on the remote possibility of an understanding with Chang Kai-shek.

label: text
text: No outbreak has been reported from the Fukien-Kwangtung border.

label: text
text: To the north of Hankow, General Tang Sung-chee, commanding the 8th army, seems to be starting another offensive against Wu Pei-flu, who is now on the Hupeh-Honan boundary.

label: text
text: The Nationalists have already nominated a council of government for Hupeh province—on the lines of that in Canton—together with other officials who include Mr. Chan Kung-pok was Foreign Commissioner and Superintendent of Customs. Mr. Chan was head of the Labour and Agricultural organisation in Canton. His place on the Boycott Conference was taken by another at the last moment owing to his being ordered to the north.

label: text
text: At the eleventh hour, Wu Peifu seems to have changed his mind as to a counter-offensive to relieve the pressure on Wuchang. There is no official news regarding the besieged city.

label: text
text: A telegram from Hankow, dated September 19, states that missionaries of all denominations in Hankow and their property are safe, but that some fighting has taken place at Chikungshan, where there are missionary and Alliance missionaries from Wuchang. Bombs have been dropped on buildings adjacent to the Alliance Mission property.—Reuter.

At the adjourned annual meeting of the China Provident, Loan & Mortgage Co., Ltd. to-day, a further postponement till November 12 was passed by the shareholders.
Mr. F. M. Crawford addressed the meeting, and asked for information for shareholders, Mr. R. G. Shewan (transpiring).

label: text
text: It is anticipated that the report of the investigation committee will be ready before November 12

label: text
text: A departure from the usual procedure of the majority of meetings of local public companies was the ending; and approval of minutes of the previous meeting.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: After the notice and last minute had been read, Mr. Shewan said:—Gentlemen,—The 29th ordinary general meeting which was held on July 22 last was adjourned until to-day at the request of the investigation Committee, pending the submission of their report.

label: text
text: I have been requested by them to move a further adjournment of this meeting, owing to the fact that their report is not yet ready for presentation.

label: text
text: I therefore beg to propose:—That this meeting of shareholders stands adjourned until Friday, November 12, 1926 at the same hour and place.

label: text
text:
Will someone kindly second that?
Mr. C. A. da Roza's seconded.

label: text
text: It is now nearly six months since the meeting in which we appointed this committee to go into the affairs of the company together with the Consulting Committee, and as they had the benefit of the preliminary investigation prior to their appointment, I cannot help but think that by this time some information might have been given to the shareholders as to the result of this investigation.

label: text
text:
On a call by the chair for remarks of shareholders, if any, Mr. F. M. Crawford said:—
While I feel sure shareholders will support me in sympathising with the members of the Investigating Committee, who are doubtless putting in a great deal of work and energy on our behalf and have more or less a thankless task before them, I would like to take this opportunity of asking for some information as to what has been done.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: In six months surely something definite should have been arrived at by the two committees acting conjointly, and it is difficult to understand why it is continually necessary to have these meetings post-

label: text
text: A glance at the Articles of Association should suffice to convince shareholders that the Consulting Committee have very little responsibility, and although they may be considered guilty to some degree of negligence, it seems quite obvious that they cannot be held liable financially for any loss.

label: text
text: Has the Investigating Committee been spending its time in trying to place the blame of past work on the Consulting Committee? If so, I shall be glad to know what the approximate cost of this investigation is going to be, for it seems to be more or less a waste of time and shareholders' money.
